summary: Deep technical session focused on Private VPC deployment networking (AWS PrivateLink, interface endpoints, NAT egress, subnets, Route53/DNS) and how those choices interact with runtime performance (latency, throughput), KV cache locality, batching, and quantization trade-offs. Action items and next steps agreed to run network benchmarks and share diagrams + docs.
topics: Interface endpoints, NLB, and cross-account considerations
Egress/NAT patterns and implications for control-plane callbacks
DNS & Route53 private hosted zones, resolver endpoints, split-horizon
Runtime considerations: KV cache locality, batching latency vs throughput, quantization impact
Network tuning: MTU, TCP window, keepalives, ENI placement
transcript: 00:00 Speaker 1 (Sara): ok hi everyone thanks for joining we wanted to walk through private vpc details and how that'll affect latency throughput and the runtime behavior

00:08 Speaker 2 (Maya): thanks sara yeah major ask from our side is low predictable latency for inference and also keeping PHI in our vpc, so PrivateLink seems like the right pattern, curious on tradeoffs

00:18 Speaker 3 (Devon): yea hi all, quick context: our private deployment runs the Redwood control plane in a customer-managed VPC via PrivateLink; inference traffic hits local model servers in your account. we'll cover where kv cache lives and how batching impacts observed p99s

00:32 Speaker 4 (Tom): question up front — does Redwood create interface endpoints in our account or do we call an endpoint in Redwood's account? mixing of cross-account endpoints is a sticking point for our security team

00:45 Speaker 2 (Devon): good call — we usually recommend cross-account interface endpoints backed by an NLB in our account, but we can also host an NLB in your account via an endpoint service. there are pros/cons: cross-account keeps control centralized but you'll need to allow the service principal and manage SG rules carefully
01:05 Speaker 5 (Priya): security — what about endpoint ENIs and security groups? we want to restrict egress to only the model servers and KMS calls to our account

01:14 Speaker 3 (Devon): the interface endpoint creates ENIs in your subnets, the SG attached to those ENIs controls inbound from your resources. outbound to Redwood's NLB is managed by the endpoint service. for KMS you can keep calls in your account by using a customer-managed CMK; Redwood supports both customer KMS and a bring-your-own-key model for Private deployments

01:37 Speaker 1 (Sara): and just to set expectations on latency: PrivateLink usually adds a small overhead vs a direct VPC-local service, typically ~1-3 ms depending on region and AZ crossing. the bigger impacts are cross-AZ ENI placement and whether traffic hairpins through a NAT or transits a proxy

01:55 Speaker 4 (Tom): hairpinning — that's a big worry. we have a pattern where subnets without NAT need to reach internet for control callbacks; how do you handle outbound admin/control-plane calls from the model servers?

02:07 Speaker 3 (Devon): good question — two patterns we see: (1) model servers run in private subnets and egress through a NAT gateway for any external callbacks (e.g., license checks, telemetry), or (2) set up VPC endpoints for the specific services so no NAT is needed. for strict no-egress policies, we can operate in a fully private mode where control-plane calls are proxied over PrivateLink back to Redwood's control plane — that requires additional cross-account setup but avoids internet egress
02:33 Speaker 5 (Priya): and DNS? We run a split-horizon Route53 setup, we need the Redwood endpoint to resolve to private ips only inside our VPC

02:41 Speaker 3 (Devon): we support Route53 private hosted zones paired with conditional forwarders. typically you create a private hosted zone in your account for redwood-inference.<yourcompany>.svc and point records at the interface endpoint IPs. if you use cross-account endpoints we share the endpoint DNS name; you can then alias an A record to the endpoint's private IP. if you need centralized DNS, you can also use resolver endpoints to forward queries to Redwood's resolver — slightly more complex to set up
03:05 Speaker 6 (Jason): performance question: does PrivateLink change SSL/TLS termination point? are we seeing extra TLS handshakes that will add CPU on the model hosts?

03:13 Speaker 3 (Devon): PrivateLink is TCP-level tunneling to the NLB; TLS may be terminated at the NLB or at the Redwoods' backend depending on your compliance needs. for low CPU overhead we can keep TLS passthrough to the model servers and offload termination to your side if you prefer. we also support mTLS between the control plane and model servers for mutual auth
03:33 Speaker 2 (Maya): runtime impact — can you talk about KV cache placement? if the cache is remote that'll add network latency and kill p95, right?

03:42 Speaker 3 (Devon): yes that's critical. our inference runtime prefers an in-process KV cache (GPU/CPU memory) for per-request prefix caching — that's local to the model server so it's millisecond-level. for sharing cache across replicas we optionally use a Redis-like shared cache; that does incur network cost and we recommend co-locating cache instances in the same AZ as the model servers to avoid cross-AZ hops. for Private deployments, we recommend hosting cache nodes in the same VPC and subnets as model servers to keep cache lookup <1ms typically
04:10 Speaker 4 (Tom): and batching — if we enable aggressive batching to increase throughput will that add tail latency for small queries?

04:17 Speaker 3 (Devon): batching tradeoff is classic: larger batch sizes increase throughput and GPU utilization but increase queueing latency. we support dynamic batching with latency SLO targets — i.e., you can configure target p95 or p99 and the runtime will hold requests up to a configured max batch window. for low-latency interactive workloads we recommend smaller max_batch_ms (5-20ms) and conservative batch caps; for high-throughput background jobs larger windows are fine

04:42 Speaker 1 (Sara): to add, quantization often helps throughput significantly — int8 or 4-bit quantized models reduce memory footprint so you can fit larger batches on a GPU, reducing per-token microseconds. but quantization can slightly change output quality, so it's a trade-off we test with your prompts
04:57 Speaker 2 (Maya): any guidance on expected throughput numbers? we run ~200 qps with typical seq length ~256 tokens, with p99 < 120 ms target

05:06 Speaker 3 (Devon): ballpark: on a single A10-like GPU with int8 and batching tuned you might see 300-600 seq-length-256 tokens qps for a medium model; p99 depends on batching and network — with local cache and co-located infra we routinely hit p99 ~80-150 ms. we will run benchmarks with your exact workload
05:24 Speaker 6 (Jason): network tuning — any specific MTU or TCP options we should set? we have had issues with fragmentation crossing NATs

05:31 Speaker 3 (Devon): set the MTU to 9001 only if your entire network path supports jumbo frames — otherwise stick to 1500. enable tcp_keepalive and proper window scaling; for long-lived HTTP streams we use HTTP/2 keepalives to avoid TLS renegotiation. also ensure your SGs allow ephemeral ports for the ENIs that back the interface endpoint
05:52 Speaker 5 (Priya): logging and audit — we need flow logs and audit trails; can Redwood ingest our VPC flow logs or do you provide logs from the model runtime?

06:00 Speaker 1 (Sara): we ingest runtime telemetry and can ship audit logs to your S3 via a cross-account role. for network-level logs, you keep VPC Flow Logs; we can correlate our request IDs with your logs if you share the flow logs — helps debug any packet-level anomalies
06:15 Speaker 4 (Tom): curious about cross-AZ latency if endpoints span multiple AZs, do we pick the nearest ENI?

06:21 Speaker 3 (Devon): interface endpoints create ENIs in the subnets you attach; your instances will use the local ENI so traffic will stay AZ-local if routed correctly. the problem is when the endpoint service's backing NLB is in a different AZ — that can cause a small cross-AZ transit. best practice: create endpoints in same AZs as your model servers and ensure NLB is configured with healthy targets in matching AZs
06:45 Speaker 2 (Maya): what about scaling model servers? when we autoscale up does the KV cache require warmup?

06:51 Speaker 3 (Devon): yes warm start matters — new replicas have cold KV caches; we mitigate with two strategies: (1) pre-warm caches via a background warmup job that replay common prefixes, and (2) sticky routing so repeated clients hit the same warmed replica for a time window. for true scale-ups you might see a short p99 spike during ramp
07:12 Speaker 6 (Jason): storage/perf — are models stored locally on instance disks or fetched from S3 on start? that affects startup latency

07:18 Speaker 3 (Devon): model shards are staged on fast instance storage (NVMe or EBS io2) at startup; if a replica needs to pull a model that's cold we stream from S3 — we recommend keeping a set of warm instances or using instance policies that keep a small warm pool for predictable latency
07:31 Speaker 2 (Maya): any known gotchas with PrivateLink and DNS resolving to 169 addresses or something odd? we had earlier a case where endpoint DNS names didn't resolve inside our corporate VPN

07:41 Speaker 3 (Devon): yes split-horizon DNS can bite you — if your corporate VPN uses its own resolver you may need Route53 resolver endpoints or conditional forwarding so the endpoint names resolve to private IPs. also watch for TTLs; some SDKs cache DNS aggressively which can hamper failover between AZs
07:57 Speaker 5 (Priya): for compliance we need to ensure no metadata leaks. do your agents call out to metadata services?

08:03 Speaker 1 (Sara): Redwood runtime avoids calling instance metadata for customer secrets; we use injected secrets via environment or a secure sidecar. for telemetry we can disable outbound telemetry entirely in Private deployments
08:16 Speaker 4 (Tom): let's talk throughput ceiling — any network-level bottlenecks to watch for?

08:21 Speaker 3 (Devon): main bottlenecks are: single NLB connection limits, per-ENI bandwidth (depends on instance type), and packet-per-second limits on small instances. pick instance types with enhanced networking (ENA) and sufficient network bandwidth; for high qps use multiple model server pods across ENIs and use the endpoint's load balancing to distribute
08:40 Speaker 2 (Maya): can Redwood recommend instance types? we run on AWS — looking at g5 or a10 families

08:46 Speaker 3 (Devon): for mixed latency/throughput g5/ a10 / h100 families are common; g5 with fp16 or a10 with int8 quantized models tend to hit good cost/latency sweet spots. we'll bring a short reference table in the follow up doc
08:58 Speaker 6 (Jason): we also need to ensure the MTU mismatch with our on-prem VPN doesn't cause fragmentation — we'll include network team in follow-up

09:05 Speaker 1 (Sara): agreed — next step we will share a 'private-vpc-checklist' that lists required SG rules, route tables, DNS entries, and minimal IAM roles. devon will include notes on KV cache and batching defaults
09:16 Speaker 2 (Maya): last quick one — what's expected monitoring surface? we need token-level latency, per-model p99s, and error traces

09:24 Speaker 3 (Devon): Redwood Console exposes per-route token/latency breakdowns, model-level traces, and you can export raw metrics to CloudWatch/Prometheus. for private deployments we can set up a CloudWatch cross-account role or push metrics to your Prometheus endpoint
09:39 Speaker 1 (Sara): ok great thanks everyone — we'll follow up with docs and schedule the perf run. any other questions?
09:45 Speaker 2 (Maya): none from me thanks
09:47 Speaker 4 (Tom): thanks all
10:00 End of recording
